Am I wrong for telling our 6 year old her dog "de-aged" rather than died? Our daughter has little concept of death. She knows what it is but has never experienced it. That is until our family dog passed at 12 years old, a little Cairn runt. She wasn't sick, or in pain or injured, it was just her time I suppose. She passed in her sleep, laying in front of our fridge.

We decided to get another puppy right away, my husband organized it in under 24 hours. He came home with a little Cairn puppy, only 10 weeks old. Same color and everything. We surprised our daughter but made it out as if we were also surprised. We explained her dog de-aged back to a puppy. We even decided to name the dog the same name. Our daughter bought it and after two weeks hasn't questioned anything.

My parents think we're setting her up for a very difficult conversation when she gets older and a skewed sense of death. On the other hand, we don't know how to approach this topic because she truly loved the dog to no end. We don't see what we've done as negative, but we'll leave this for others to judge.
base: You're in the wrong. Not only are you setting your daughter up for all sorts of problems, you're disrespecting the 12 years you had with the original dog. Was the dog not a valued member of your family that you can just replace her and pretend it's the same dog? And all of this because you don't know how to talk to your daughter about a tough subject? What's going to happen when you need to discuss sex or drugs? Or when a grandparent dies and she wonders why they didn't just "de-age" like the dog? And when she inevitably does find out the truth she won't trust you or believe what you say anymore. Grow up and be a d*** parent.

But replacing the dog and telling her it "de-aged" is likely to create more confusion and hurt later. It also overlooks the 12 years you had with the original dog, who was a valued family member in her own right.

Children need age-appropriate, honest explanations of death, even when those conversations are difficult. Otherwise, when a grandparent dies or another hard subject comes up, she may reasonably wonder why they cannot "de-age" too. It is your spouse asking you to sit with her and your child, light candles, exchange a small gift, eat food, or otherwise support a tradition that matters to her. You can set reasonable boundaries: you do not have to pray, profess beliefs you do not hold, attend synagogue, or pretend to be Jewish. But participating as a supportive husband and father is different from being forced to adopt a religion.

post: Am I wrong for using the shoulder as a really long turn lane? Every day on my way home from work, I go to the gym. Once and a while the timing of the traffic light past the gym gets messed up and rush hour traffic will back up about 500 feet past my gym's entrance for a few weeks until it's fixed. During these times, since I'm turning into the gym well before the problem traffic light anyway, I use the hurricane lane/shoulder to get to the gym instead of waiting the 3 light cycles (~8 min) it would take to get there otherwise. I assumed it was ok since plenty of other people do it and it's not like I'm inconveniencing anyone. Plus, I'm wasting gas by idling. base:
You're slightly in the wrong.

- The shoulder is for emergencies and, in many places, using it to bypass traffic is illegal. Drivers (and emergency vehicles) expect it to be clear, and people pull out from driveways assuming no one's speeding along it. It's a safety risk, not just an etiquette issue.
- It's also queue-jumping. Everyone else is waiting through the same bad light; using the shoulder for 500 feet to skip the line isn't fair, even if it feels harmless and others are doing it.
- Saving a few minutes or some idling gas doesn't outweigh the risk or the rules.

That said, your coworker reporting your plate to your boss instead of just minding their business or, if they were truly concerned, reporting it to the city/police, is pretty petty. But on the narrow question-using the shoulder that way-you shouldn't do it.

Better options:
- Report the signal timing to the city/transportation department or 311 so it gets fixed faster.
- Take an alternate route, turn earlier, or adjust timing if you can.
- Only use a shoulder/right-side area if it's clearly marked as a legal right-turn lane near the intersection.

base:

She expressed an interest in getting her nose pierced but I managed to convince her it would look unprofessional (her career is very important to her).

Am I wrong?
base:
This isn't really about tattoos. It's about control.

"Convincing" her not to get a nose piercing wasn't a mutual decision; it was you leveraging her insecurities about her career to get your way. She's told you flat out that she's held off on things she wants for years because of your reaction, not because she changed her mind. That's not compromise, that's a person shrinking themselves to keep the peace in their own marriage.

And now you're doing it again-telling her it would "affect your attraction to her," which is just a softer way of saying "do this and I'll punish you by withdrawing affection." That's coercive, even if you don't intend it that way.

You are not entitled to veto power over her skin, and you're not entitled to guilt her out of things she wants by acting like her body is a shared asset you get to manage.

Am I wrong for asking my mom to fill up the car w/ gas? I [19M] am currently at home for my uni's reading week.

Today, I need the car to get somewhere later tonight, and I asked my mom to use the car. She told me it's low on gas and that before I leave I should fill up.

So my mom just told me that she's going to a hair salon to get her hair cut and I said to her

"Oh, do you mind filling up the tank if you're going out anyways?"

she told me no, "you do it".

When I asked for a reason why she just said "you do it"

If you're going out anyways, why not just fill up the tank? I really don't understand her logic, I even offered to let her use my gas speed pass so that she doesn't even have to pay. She still said no, the thing that makes me so angry is that she just doesn't want to go out of her way to get the gas because she's just so damn lazy.

She's saying I'm being a huge jerk, and that I'M the one who needs the extra gas, so I need to get it. She is now telling me since I'm being so lazy, I'm no longer allowed to use the car, and to bus 1.2 hours to get where I need to go.

My bro is also telling me that I'm being a jerk since it's her car, but with everything I offered- and the fact that she's going out anyways Am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

It's her car. She told you to fill it up before you leave with it. Instead of just doing that simple task, you tried to offload it onto her because she happened to be going out too. Then when she said no, you pushed back and asked her to justify why she wouldn't do a favor for you.

Think about it from her side: it's her car, her responsibility technically falls to you since you're the one borrowing it and were already told to handle the gas. You offering your gas card doesn't really change the core issue - you're still asking her to spend her time and make an extra stop to accommodate your errand, on her way to get her hair done, because you didn't want to be bothered.

"She's going out anyways" isn't really the slam-dunk logic you think it is. People don't automatically owe you a detour just because they're already leaving the house. She's not your chauffeur or personal assistant.

Calling your own mom "lazy" for not wanting to run your errand for you, when she's already loaning you her car and had already told you to gas it up yourself, is pretty entitled. The fact that your brother is also telling you that you're in the wrong is a good sign you should listen.

You're not being asked to bus 1.2 hours as some cruel punishment - you're being asked to take responsibility for the very small task you were already assigned.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong, I think.

It's her car, and she'd already asked you to fill it up before you left with it. Instead of just doing that, it sounds like you tried to hand the task to her because she happened to be going out too. When she said no, you pushed her to justify it.

I get why "she's going out anyways" felt like it should settle things for you - but I don't think it works quite that way from her side. It's still her time and an extra stop, on her way to get her hair done, for something that was already your task. Offering your gas card is a nice gesture, but it doesn't really change who the errand belongs to.

Calling her "lazy" for not wanting to take that on, when she's already lending you the car and had already told you to handle the gas yourself, comes across as a bit entitled. And it seems worth noting that your brother sees it the same way - that's probably worth sitting with.

Honestly, the ask here isn't that big - it's the same small task you were already given, just now with a bus ride attached because of how the conversation went.

title: Am I wrong for not listening to my wife complain? This whole thing is the kind of super petty things married couples get
post:
Am I wrong for not listening to my wife complain? This whole thing is the kind of super petty things married couples get into.

I was annoyed with our old vacuum so I bought a new one. When I got it I asked my wife to try it out and tell me what she thought of it. If she didn't like it I'd return it. She refused to try it saying she didn't care.

Fast forward a month. I've been using it daily and she still hasn't tried it. I'm out one day or something and she finally has to use it.

That evening she comes up to me and says 'I'm definitely not saying we should return the vacuum, but -'.

At this point I cut her off and say 'sorry, but I'd rather not hear about it'. She of course gets mad and I point out she had a month to try it out and that I asked for her opinion and she refused, so I'm no longer interested in hearing about it.

Am I wrong for cutting her off?
base:
You're in the wrong. Here, and I think you know it on some level.

Your wife wasn't asking you to return the vacuum. She explicitly said she wasn't asking for that. She was doing the completely normal relationship thing of sharing a reaction to something she just experienced. That's not "complaining that violates the terms of an agreement," that's just... talking to your spouse about your day.

The "you had a month to try it and didn't" argument doesn't really hold up either. Her not testing it proactively a month ago has nothing to do with whether she's allowed to have an opinion the first time she actually uses it. People don't lose the right to react to things because of a timing technicality.

Also, cutting someone off mid-sentence with "I'd rather not hear about it" is just a shutdown move. Even if you were annoyed, there were about a dozen better ways to handle it-"can we talk about this later" or actually just listening to a 30-second thought about a vacuum.

This reads less like a vacuum dispute and more like you were looking for an excuse to not engage, and the vacuum thing gave you a technicality to hide behind. That's the part that'll actually cause a fight, not the appliance.
rewrite:
I think you're in the wrong here, though I get why it felt like a "gotcha" moment in the moment.

You're right that she didn't try it when you first asked, and I get why that was frustrating - you did ask for her input up front and she passed on it. That part's fair to be annoyed about.

But it seems like what she was doing this time wasn't really "complaining" in the way you're framing it - she opened with "I'm not saying we should return it," which sounds like she was just sharing a reaction to something she'd actually just experienced, not relitigating the return decision. Those feel like different things to me: her not testing it proactively a month ago doesn't really cancel her ability to have a thought about it the first time she uses it.

I'd also gently push back on the "cut her off" part. Even granting that you were annoyed and felt like you'd already heard enough vacuum talk, "I'd rather not hear about it" mid-sentence is a pretty hard shutdown. Something like "can we talk about this later" would've gotten you the same result without the sting.

If I'm honest, it reads a little like the month-old technicality gave you a reason to disengage rather than the actual cause of it. That's probably the piece worth looking at - not the vacuum, but the moment you decided not to listen.

You didn't approach a celebrity, you approached a stranger who's become an object of mass ridicule and controversy, and asked to use her for content/a story to tell. That's true whether she said yes or not.

Her mom "grumbling the entire time" should have been your signal to read the room. People experiencing unwanted infamy don't usually love being recognized in public by strangers on vacation, even if they're too polite (or worn down) to say no.

You can be fascinated by a legal case or a public controversy without treating a random woman and her mother like an attraction to collect during your trip. Your SO isn't wrong to be embarrassed. Ask yourself how you'd feel if you were dealing with a humiliating internet-famous moment in your life and someone excitedly asked for a selfie with you and your mom while she stood there stone-faced.

But what really made me mad was that he was giving me the cold shoulder particularly bad and talking to this girl instead. So I walked away to get a drink, and my boyfriend's friend came up to me. I told him to calm down, that I was just teasing him giving him a taste of his own medicine, but that really set him off. base:

Deliberately flirting with his friend to get back at him for talking to another girl isn't "teasing" or giving him "a taste of his own medicine" - it's manipulative. You weren't communicating your hurt feelings, you were staging a reaction. That's a passive-aggressive way to handle jealousy, and it's understandable why it blew up the way it did. If you were hurt that he was cold to you and chatting up someone else, the move is to say "hey, what's going on, you're acting weird and it's making me feel bad" - not orchestrate a counter-flirtation as payback.

So yes, on the immediate question: you engineered a situation to provoke a reaction, and it worked exactly as intended, just with more heat than you wanted.

But separately - he pushed you. That's not "he got upset," that's a physical escalation that has nothing to do with who was pettier first. Being jealous or hurt doesn't justify shoving your partner. That's the part of this story I'd actually be more concerned about long-term, more than who was in the wrong for the party drama.

So: you're in the wrong for playing games instead of just talking to him, but that doesn't make what he did to you okay. Two separate issues, and the second one is the more serious one.

title: Am I wrong for "outing" my younger sister? My mom and I were talking and I casually referred to my sister's girlfriend a
post:
Am I wrong for "outing" my younger sister? My mom and I were talking and I casually referred to my sister's girlfriend as girlfriend. I didn't think anything of it, they behave as more than friends around her and it seemed obvious to me and everyone that they were in a relationship. Furthermore, my mom is very accepting and hasn't done anything to suggest any intolerance of their relationship.

My sister overheard and messaged me that I am "awful for thinking I have the right to tell our mom that", saying its obvious she hasn't talked to our mom about their relationship. She essentially feels like me referring to her gf as gf was outing her to my mom.

I disagree that it's obvious she hasn't talked to my mom about their relationship because the way they behave around her is no different than any other young couple. My mom definitely recognized the relationship was different from a friendship, she called them "cute" to me previously.

I didn't think labeling her as a gf was out of line considering she is in a romantic relationship with my sister, but what does reddit think, Am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong, and I think you know it on some level or you wouldn't be asking.

Here's the thing: it doesn't matter that your mom is accepting. It doesn't matter that the relationship seemed obvious. It doesn't matter that your mom already called them "cute." None of that changes the fundamental issue, which is that it wasn't your information to confirm or deny out loud.

Your sister gets to decide when, how, and to whom she discloses her relationship status and orientation. Even if your mom had 99% already figured it out, there's a real difference between "I have a strong suspicion" and having someone else state it as fact. You took that choice away from her and made it for her, in real time, without asking.

Your reasoning ("it seemed obvious to everyone," "she's accepting anyway") is the exact justification almost everyone uses after they out someone. It might even be true! But that's not really the point. The point is your sister had not yet decided to say it herself, and now she doesn't get to. You collapsed the timeline she was working on, whatever that timeline was and for whatever reasons she had (even if those reasons don't make total sense to you).

You also don't actually know that she hadn't talked to your mom about it in some other way, or that she wasn't planning to soon, or that there wasn't a specific reason she wanted to be the one to say the word "girlfriend" out loud first. That's information you don't have access to, which is exactly why it wasn't your call.

A genuine apology here isn't "sorry you're upset" or "I still think I was justified but sorry." It's "I shouldn't have said that, it wasn't mine to share, I'm sorry."

I get that your mom is accepting, that the relationship seemed obvious to everyone, and that she'd even called them "cute" before. Those are all fair points, and I don't doubt any of them. But I don't think they change the core issue: it wasn't your information to confirm out loud.

If you want to smooth things over, I think it'd help to lead with something like "I shouldn't have said that, it wasn't mine to share, I'm sorry" rather than "sorry you're upset" or "sorry, but I still think I was right" - even if you still feel your read on the situation was reasonable.

base:

You cherry-picked one word out of a proper noun/compound term to try to retroactively justify your answer.

This isn't really a pedantic technicality on their part - it's the actual answer printed on the card. If you'd said "water ice" that's arguably a discussion worth having. But you said "water," which is meaningfully different from "ice" in a trivia context, especially about a specific NASA discovery.

Beyond the rules-lawyering, the bigger issue is your reaction. Raging at a casual family game night over a Trivial Pursuit ruling is disproportionate. Even if you felt strongly you were right, family game night is supposed to be fun and low-stakes. Escalating to "raging" over a board game answer - even a legitimately close call - is going to make you the person who ruins game night, not the person who was robbed of a correct answer.

Take the L on this one, and maybe apologize for the reaction even if you still privately think your answer had merit.

title: Am I wrong: Found pregnant coworker's misplaced cigarettes, and threw them away rather than returning them? Pretty strai
post: Am I wrong: Found pregnant coworker's misplaced cigarettes, and threw them away rather than returning them? Pretty straight forward. Just unsure if I was right to throw them away or return them. It is HER body and child and HER possessions but I don't think I could've brought myself to hand cigarettes to a pregnant woman. She's about 4 Mo. pregnant and 24 years old
base:
You're in the wrong.

I get the instinct-but this isn't your call to make. She's an adult, it's her body, her pregnancy, her legal property. Throwing away someone's belongings without consent isn't "help," it's a unilateral decision that you had the right to overrule her autonomy because you disagreed with her choices. That's true even when the stakes feel high to you.

A few things to sit with:
- You don't actually know her full situation-cutting down, occasional smoker, stress relapse, etc. Nicotine addiction is brutal, especially compounded with pregnancy hormones and possibly a partner/family who smokes too.
- Throwing them away doesn't stop her from smoking. It just means she now has to notice they're missing, wonder if she misplaced them, maybe feel a flash of anxiety, and then go buy more. You haven't protected the baby; you've just added a layer of confusion/gaslighting to her day and wasted her money.
- If you're this concerned, the honest move would've been to talk to her directly-not confiscate her stuff secretly. Secretly taking someone's property "for their own good" isn't kindness, it's overstepping.

Good on you for planning to come clean and repay her-that's the right move and will probably go over better than you expect, especially if you're honest and not preachy about it. Own it as what it was: well-intentioned but not okay.

That's true even when the worry behind it feels urgent.

That said, it sounds like you've already thought this through since posting-planning to be upfront with her and pay her back is a good call, and I'd guess it'll go over better than you're expecting if you're straightforward about it. I'd just frame it to yourself as: well-intentioned, but not something you were entitled to decide for her.

title: Am I wrong for getting mad at my girlfriend for eating our poutine? This happened last night. My friends, my girlfriend

We decided to stop at Smokes Poutine to get a nice triple pork. So we all get our food and then decide to walk home and eat when we get there.

Here's the thing: you were all drunk, cold, and hungry, and someone (your girlfriend) made the very human decision to start eating food that smelled amazing while walking. That's not some huge betrayal-that's just what happens when you're intoxicated and impatient with hot food in your hands.

Your actual complaint boils down to:

2. The poutine got cold

But you have to ask yourself-was she actually slowing down significantly, or were you just irritated and looking for a reason to be annoyed? A 5-minute walk becoming a 6 or 7-minute walk in -10 degrees isn't the tragedy you're framing it as.

Also, it's her poutine too. You shared it, you're a couple, this isn't some sacred artifact she desecrated. If she was hungry and wanted to start eating, that's a pretty normal impulse that doesn't deserve genuine anger.

Getting a little annoyed? Sure, that's understandable in the moment. But "getting mad" at your girlfriend over communal poutine consumption during a drunk night out is the kind of thing that's going to sound absurd to you tomorrow (and honestly sounds a little absurd now).

Eat the cold poutine, laugh about it, move on. This is not the hill to die on.

title: Am I wrong for not calling my sister by her preferred name?
post:
Am I wrong for not calling my sister by her preferred name?
My sister(now 25) has never liked her name and insists on us calling her a name she likes that she's chosen, however she refuses to change her name legally. I (23 M) told her I will call her by her legal name, whatever that may be.

The reason for this is because I don't believe she is serious about changing her name and think she's just don't it for attention and to seem quirky. Though out our childhood she has had various names that she "likes" at the time, which I have used and stuck to, but changes after a while when she gets bored of it or changes her mind. For the last 3ish years she has instead on a particular name but I've told her if she's really serious about it, pick a name, change it legally and I will go along with it. I'm tired of getting used to a name (5th one now) her for to only change it not long after.

Am I wrong for not going along with her current name?
base:
You're in the wrong, with some understanding for why you feel this way.

Here's the thing: needing a legal name change as "proof" of seriousness isn't really a fair bar. Legal name changes cost money, require paperwork, court dates in some places, updating IDs/documents, etc. Plenty of people go by a different name for years - sometimes their whole life - without ever legally changing it, for all kinds of valid reasons (cost, family pressure, uncertainty about whether they want to fully commit, or just not seeing the need since a legal document doesn't determine who they are).

Your frustration about the pattern of switching names 5 times is understandable - that's genuinely hard to keep up with, and it's fair to feel tired of relearning. But the current name has stuck for 3 years, which is a pretty long stretch. That's not really "still deciding" territory anymore.

Making legal paperwork the condition for you to respect what she wants to be called comes across less like reasonable pushback and more like a power move - basically saying "I won't take you seriously until you jump through a hoop I've decided matters." Names carry real weight for how people feel seen by their family, and continuing to use a name she's told you she doesn't want, especially now that it's been consistent for years, is going to read as disrespectful no matter how you frame the "logic" behind it.

If the switching bothered you, that would've been a fair thing to express years ago. But now that it's stable, the legal-name ultimatum feels like you're holding onto old resentment more than reacting to her current behavior.

title: Am I wrong for thinking that I am allowed to insult my friends opinions I recently had a little head butt with my friend

Am I wrong for thinking that I am allowed to insult my friends opinions I recently had a little head butt with my friend over a discussion on politics. While we were talking I insulted his opinion calling it stupid. After I said this he essentially said that I am not allowed to criticize his opinions and that disagreements should just be dropped whenever they come up. I personally disagree and while I am the type of person that thinks constant bickering and arguments over trivial nonsense is unnecessary I also believe I am allowed to criticize him if I want to. And throughout all of this if he decides to insult my comments from time to time I believe it is acceptable too. In no shape or form was this harassment or continued insults it was just once. He is in every way entitled to believe whatever he wants and I am entitled to call it dumb.

So, AMITA?
base:
You're in the wrong, but let's be precise about why, because you're conflating two different things: having opinions and disagreements versus insulting someone.

You're right that you're allowed to disagree with your friend. You're right that you're allowed to criticize his opinion, explain why you think he's wrong, argue the point, whatever. That's normal discourse between friends who trust each other enough to disagree.

But "criticizing an opinion" and "calling it stupid" are not the same thing. One is engaging with the substance of what someone said. The other is a dismissive insult that shuts down actual discussion and just makes the other person feel belittled. You can say "I think you're wrong because X" without saying "that's stupid." The fact that you're framing this as "I'm allowed to criticize him" when what you actually did was insult him tells me you already know the distinction but are choosing to blur it because it makes your behavior look more defensible.

Also, "if he decides to insult me back sometimes, that's acceptable too" is a pretty telling standard to set. You're basically saying insults are fine as long as they're occasional and mutual, which just means you've agreed to a friendship where you periodically get to be a jerk to each other and call it normal.

Your friend didn't say you can't disagree with him or that all conflict must be avoided. He said don't insult his opinions. That's a completely reasonable boundary, and you calling his opinion "stupid" is exactly the behavior he was asking you to stop.

I tried to slowly text her less and less and asking her for dates less, to make myself less interesting/ 'loveable'. I did not want to hurt her feelings by ending it while she was still very in love with me. This went on for about 3 months before i finally decided the one-sided relationship had gone on for too long and I broke up with her. It turned out that she was still very much in love with me, same as when we first started dating. I just kept her on a leash for 3 months trying to make her fell out of love with me, the same way I fell out with her, but instead i might've hurt her more than when I had just broken up when I had nothing but friendly feelings for her... I believe i did the right thing by trying not to make her first break up that hard, but my friends are telling i should have ended it immediately so we could both move on. am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong. Here, though I don't think your intentions were malicious.

What you did was string someone along for 3 months while slowly withdrawing, hoping she'd catch feelings-fatigue on her own timeline instead of just being honest with her. That's not kindness, even though I believe you thought it was. Real kindness would have been telling her directly: "I've noticed I'm losing romantic feelings, and I think we should talk about where this is going." That gives her actual information to work with and the agency to process it in real time.

Instead, you unilaterally decided you knew what was best for her emotional journey and tried to engineer her feelings without her consent or knowledge. You spent three months making her feel like something was wrong with her, or with the relationship, without ever naming it. She probably sensed the distance and had no idea why, which is arguably worse than a clean breakup because at least clean breakups come with clarity.

The outcome proves this: she was just as in love with you at the end as at the beginning. Your plan didn't work, and worse, it likely added confusion and self-doubt to what was already going to be a painful experience for her.

Your friends are right. When you know you're done, the respectful thing is to end it clearly and let both people grieve and move on. Slow-fading someone isn't gentler, it just delays and often intensifies the pain, and it takes away the other person's ability to understand what's happening to their own relationship.

I have two little sisters and a little brother who are all capable of cleaning and they don't work. I'm not gonna lie I don't work everyday but I do go to school as well. So Am I wrong?
base:
Here's an honest take: you're in the wrong, but mildly, and it's fixable.

Here's the thing - paying bills and doing chores aren't actually substitutes for each other. They're different contributions to a household, and living in a home involves both financial upkeep AND physical upkeep. The fact that you contribute money doesn't mean the dishes stop needing to be washed or the bathroom stops needing to be cleaned. Someone still has to do it, and "I paid for groceries so I shouldn't have to help cook" isn't really how shared living works.

That said, your frustration isn't baseless. It sounds like the real issue is fairness among siblings - you're working, going to school, AND contributing financially, while your younger siblings do none of that and also skip chores. That's a legitimate grievance. If that's true, the fix isn't "I pay so I'm exempt," it's "everyone who lives here does age-appropriate chores, and it's not fair that I'm doing more of everything."

A few things worth sitting with:
- Does your mom actually need that money from you, or is this more about teaching responsibility? That changes the conversation a lot.
- "I go to school" is valid, but so is "I clean the bathroom once a week" - these aren't mutually exclusive.
- The stronger, more persuasive argument to your mom isn't "I pay so I shouldn't clean," it's "It's unfair that I'm contributing money AND chores while my siblings do neither."

You're not the world's biggest jerk here, but the "I pay, therefore I'm exempt" logic is where you're losing the argument - and probably why your mom pushed back hard.
rewrite:
I think you're slightly in the wrong, but honestly a pretty fixable one.

I hear you that you're contributing financially, going to school, and it feels like your siblings get a pass while you're doing more of everything - that frustration seems real and worth taking seriously.

That said, I think paying bills and doing chores aren't really substitutes for each other. They're just different kinds of contributions to a household, and living somewhere tends to involve both. The money you put in doesn't make the dishes or the bathroom stop needing attention - someone still has to do that work, and "I paid for groceries so I shouldn't have to help cook" isn't quite how shared living usually works.

A couple things that might be worth sitting with:
- Does your mom actually need that money from you, or is part of this about her wanting you to build responsibility? That might change how you think about the ask.
- "I go to school" is a real constraint, but it doesn't necessarily rule out something small and consistent, like handling the bathroom once a week.
- I think the stronger case to make to your mom isn't "I pay, so I shouldn't have to clean" - it's "It's not fair that I'm contributing money and chores while my siblings do neither." That's the actual issue, and it's a legitimate one.

You're not the villain here, but I think the "I pay, therefore I'm exempt" framing is where the argument loses ground - and probably why your mom pushed back so hard.

title: Would I be wrong if I asked my sister not to give her baby the same name as my husband's dead brother So my husband had
post:
Would I be wrong if I asked my sister not to give her baby the same name as my husband's dead brother So my husband had a brother but, sadly, he passed away at the age of 8. My husband was 7. He had leukemia. His parents had another baby a year after he died and they gave that baby the same name. They also have the same birthday. Anyway, his younger brother was sick as a baby and they were advised to change the name because it's a baby omen. His younger brother has a different name now. So my sister is due in May and my husband's dead brother's name is on the list of names. I don't want my future nephew to have a name with this history. My sister knows the whole story about my husband's brothers and the name.

So Would I be wrong if I asked her to remove the name from her list of names? Prepared to be in the wrong because it's their kid and they can name it whatever they want
base:
This is a tricky one, but I don't think you'd be in the wrong for having a conversation about it - you would be in the wrong if you demanded or pushed hard after she's heard you out.

You have a legitimate personal connection to this name. It's not that you dislike the name aesthetically or have a random superstition - your husband watched his brother die at age 7, then his parents replaced that child with a same-named sibling with the same birthday, and THAT child got sick too until they changed his name. That's a genuinely heavy, painful family history, not just "baby omen" folklore you picked up somewhere.

It's reasonable to:
- Tell your sister once, clearly, why this name carries weight for your husband specifically
- Explain that it's not about telling her how to parent, but that you're asking as family who lived through this
- Let her know it might be hard for your husband to hear that name directed at a new baby, given his history

It's NOT reasonable to:
- Repeatedly bring it up if she says no
- Get cold or resentful toward her or the baby if she keeps the name
- Frame it as "you HAVE to remove it" rather than "please consider removing it"

Ultimately it is her child and her choice. But sharing real, personal trauma around a specific name isn't the same as generic name-shaming. She might not have fully considered how it would land for your husband emotionally, separate from the "omen" angle.

Have the conversation once, be honest about why it matters to your husband, then respect whatever she decides. If she keeps the name, that's her right, and you'll need to make peace with it for the sake of the relationship.
rewrite:
I think you wouldn't be in the wrong for having this conversation with her - it seems like you'd only be in the wrong if you pushed hard or kept bringing it up after she's heard you out.

You mentioned you're prepared to be told this is their kid and their choice, and I think that's a fair thing to hold onto. It is ultimately her decision to make. But I'd also say you have a legitimate personal connection to this name here, not just a random superstition. Your husband watched his brother die at age 7, then his parents named the next child the same name with the same birthday, and that child got sick too until they changed his name. That's a heavy, specific family history, not just "baby omen" folklore.

So it seems reasonable to:
- Tell your sister once, clearly, why this name carries weight for your husband specifically
- Frame it as sharing something painful as family who lived through it, not as instructions on how to parent
- Let her know it might be hard for your husband to hear that name on a new baby, given what he went through

It probably wouldn't land well to:
- Bring it up again and again if she says no
- Go cold or resentful toward her or the baby if she keeps the name
- Say "you have to remove it" instead of "please consider it"

She may not have fully weighed how this would feel for your husband emotionally, apart from the omen angle, so it's worth naming that clearly once. After that, I think the kindest path is to be honest with her, then really let her decide and make peace with whatever she chooses, for the relationship's sake.

title: Am I wrong for kicking my sister out of my wedding during the reception? Throwaway for obvious reasons.
post:
Am I wrong for kicking my sister out of my wedding during the reception? Throwaway for obvious reasons.

I got married last Saturday. Hooray for me! My sister was my maid of honor. During her speech, she brought up her depression and how my husband supported her through it and how "in that moment, I knew he was the one for throwaway..." (so cliche!). I thought her speech was really selfish. I think it's super inappropriate to bring up a mental illness during a wedding speech. Not only that, but the entire speech was about her. At MY wedding. 90% of the guests congratulated her afterwards and talked about how "strong" she was. Nobody was paying attention to me, at my own wedding! Sorry if I sound selfish, but IMO there is a time and a place for this sort of thing. So after the guests all greeted her, I asked her to leave and told her she was being disruptive and selfish. She was really upset but just left without arguing. My parents agree with me. but my husband and all of my close friends think I was way too harsh. Am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

Your sister didn't hijack your wedding; she used a personal, vulnerable story to illustrate what an incredible, compassionate man your husband is and why she knew he was the right partner for you.

Using a personal anecdote to show the groom's character is a very standard Maid of Honor speech format. Even if you felt bringing up mental illness was too heavy for a wedding, her intent was clearly to honor your husband and celebrate your marriage.

Here is why your reaction makes you in the wrong:

1. The guests' reaction was normal human empathy, not a betrayal. Guests spending a few minutes telling her she was brave doesn't mean your entire wedding was ruined or that you weren't the center of attention for the other 95% of the day.
2. Kicking her out solved nothing. The speech was already over. Kicking your own sister-your Maid of Honor-out of the reception was purely punitive, driven by jealousy and resentment that the spotlight shifted away from you for a brief moment.
3. Your husband disagrees with you. The story was about him being a supportive brother-in-law, and even he thinks you went way too far.
4. She left quietly. If she were truly a selfish drama queen trying to make the day about herself, she would have caused a massive scene when you kicked her out. Instead, she took the high road and left.

You let your insecurity and obsession with having 100% of the attention ruin a milestone moment and deeply damage your relationship with your sister. You owe her a massive apology.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong.

I understand your perspective, and I agree that bringing up topics like mental illness can sometimes feel heavy or out of place during a wedding celebration. It is completely natural to want your wedding day to remain focused on your new marriage.

However, it seems that your sister's intention was not to hijack your day, but rather to use a vulnerable personal story to illustrate what a compassionate and supportive man your husband is and why she knew he was the right partner for you. Sharing an anecdote to highlight the groom's character is a very standard format for a Maid of Honor speech.

Here is why your response was too harsh:

 The guests' reaction was brief empathy: Guests taking a few moments to offer kind words to your sister does not mean the entire day stopped being about you and your husband. It was just a natural, momentary human reaction.
 Asking her to leave did not resolve the situation: Because the speech had already ended, having your sister and Maid of Honor leave the reception was purely punitive.
 Your husband's perspective is important: The story directly involved your husband being a caring brother-in-law, and he also felt that kicking her out went too far.
 She handled the exit gracefully: Rather than creating a disruption or arguing, she respected your request and left quietly.

While it is understandable to feel sensitive about the focus shifting at your reception, asking your sister to leave caused unnecessary harm to your relationship. To help move forward and repair that bond, it would be best to offer her a sincere apology.

title: Am I wrong for not checking my phone A couple weeks ago I had a wedding to attend. A friend of mine was having a cookout
post:
Am I wrong for not checking my phone A couple weeks ago I had a wedding to attend. A friend of mine was having a cookout and casual reception at his house with setup the night before. The wedding fell on my wedding anniversary.

My wife was planning to stay home with our three kids and I told her I was just going to go to the 11am ceremony and then come home so we could all do something as a family. The kids had a birthday party to go to so it worked out.

Well time got away from me and I ended up staying until midnight. I checked my phone as I was leaving and saw a couple of missed calls and texts from my wife, wondering what was going on. Turns out she had also called a mutual friend who had been at the wedding, but they had left around 3pm so didn't have any news for her.

Wife is unbelievably angry. I told her I didn't have cell service inside - the place has a metal roof. She thinks I'm full of stuff and is mad that I didn't take the initiative to go outside for better service.

Am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong. Massively.

Here is a breakdown of why:

1. It was your wedding anniversary: You left your wife at home to solo-parent your three children all day and night on your own anniversary, after specifically telling her you would be home shortly after the 11:00 AM ceremony.
2. "Time got away from me" does not cover 12 hours: An 11:00 AM ceremony means you should have been home around 1:00 PM or 2:00 PM at the latest. Staying until midnight is not a minor slip of time-it is an entire half of a day. The sun literally set, afternoon turned into night, and at no point did you think, "Hey, it's 7:00 PM, I told my wife I'd be home hours ago on our anniversary"?
3. You caused genuine panic: Your wife was so worried about your whereabouts that she had to call a mutual friend to find out if you were okay. Leaving a spouse completely in the dark for 12+ hours when they expect you home in two is terrifying.
4. The "metal roof" excuse is insulting: The issue isn't that your phone had bad reception; the issue is that you never tried to check in. If you had stepped outside at 1:00 PM, 3:00 PM, or 6:00 PM to call her, you would have realized you had no service and found a way to reach her. Blaming the building's roof ignores the fact that you completely forgot your family and your commitments for 13 hours.

You completely blew off your anniversary, abandoned your wife with three kids for the entire day, vanished without communication, and are now making excuses instead of taking accountability.

You owe your wife a massive, unreserved apology, with zero excuses about cell reception.
rewrite:
I think you're in the wrong in this situation.

I acknowledge that you felt time got away from you during the event and that the building's metal roof blocked your cell reception. I also agree with you that the plan you set was to attend the 11:00 AM ceremony and then return home so you could spend your anniversary together as a family with your three kids.

However, staying until midnight meant leaving your wife to solo-parent all day and evening without any updates, which understandably caused her enough worry that she felt she needed to call a mutual friend to find out where you were. While time can sometimes slip by at social gatherings, twelve hours is a very long stretch to go without checking in. The core issue seems to be that stepping outside at some point during the day to check your phone would have allowed you to stay in touch and follow through on the plans you made.

Taking full accountability and offering her a sincere, unreserved apology-without focusing on the cell reception-would be the most positive step forward to address the situation.

title: Am I wrong for ruining my friend's pickle eating experience? I had a friend over a few weeks ago and got up to grab a be

Am I wrong for ruining my friend's pickle eating experience? I had a friend over a few weeks ago and got up to grab a beer. I noticed the jar of pickles in the fridge and decided I could go for some crunch, called out "Hey, you want a pickle?" "Sure."

I come back into the living room with the beer and two pickles, hand him one.

"Can I have a plate, knife and fork?"

"What for?"

"It's how I like to eat my pickles."

"Seriously?"

"Yeah."

"... Seriously?"

"Yes."

"It's a pickle. It's one pickle."

"That's how I like 'em."

"I mean... Sorry, but no"

"Wow."

"Wow? Hold up, you're offended?"

"sigh I don't know man, it kind of goes against the rules of being a good host."

"Right. Just one thing. When you asked for a plate, knife, and fork, were you planning on washing those?"

"Wow. Really?"

"Were you?"

"Of course not."

"Right. So let me get this straight, what's implied here is you want me, expect me, to wash three items of dishes later so that you can eat one pickle. To be a good host."

"Yeah, I guess."

"You look offended. Am I in the wrong here?"

So, was I?
base:
You're in the wrong (though this is a hilarious, low-stakes situation).

Here is why:

1. Pickles are wet and messy: Handing someone a whole, dripping pickle in a living room without at least a napkin or a small plate is already risky for your furniture and their hands.
2. Basic hosting etiquette: When you host someone and offer them food, providing basic tableware upon request is standard. Yes, eating a whole pickle with a knife and fork is eccentric, but it's not an unreasonable or difficult request to fulfill.
3. The dishwashing argument was petty: You made a stand over washing a single plate, a knife, and a fork. That takes roughly 20 seconds to rinse and put in the dishwasher or wash by hand. Cross-examining your guest with "Were you planning on washing those?" was needlessly combative and patronizing.

Your friend has a quirky way of eating pickles. The normal, hospitable reaction is to laugh, give him a hard time playfully, hand him the plate and fork, and watch him eat a pickle like a Victorian aristocrat. Instead, you turned a 10-second favor into a hostile standoff.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong, though it seems like a very funny, low-stakes situation overall.

I can certainly understand your perspective: to you, creating three dirty dishes for a single snack seems unnecessary, and I agree that eating a pickle with a knife and fork is definitely an eccentric preference.

However, it still seems that you were in the wrong here for a few reasons:

1. Pickles are often wet and messy: Handing someone a whole pickle in a living room without a plate or napkin can easily lead to dripping on hands or furniture, so wanting a barrier is fairly practical.
2. Standard hospitality includes basic tableware: Even though his preference is quirky, being a welcoming host usually involves accommodating simple requests for dishes and cutlery.
3. The reaction felt a bit combative: Asking him if he planned to wash the dishes seemed needlessly sharp over something that takes roughly twenty seconds to rinse or load into a dishwasher.

In situations like this, it is usually much better to just share a laugh, playfully tease him about his formal eating style, and hand over the plate and fork so you can both enjoy the hangout.

Am I wrong for Lady refuses to give us money but gives it to this other guy Am I wrong: Kinda "are we wrong". This is my family's story.

Characters involve: Me-me Dad-D Mom-M Sister-S Bitch-B

We need to go to this store to cash a check. D walks ahead from the rest of us, since they stop cashing checks at 8:00. It's 7:59. The rest of us walk in at 8:00, and D tells us they won't cash his check because "We close at 8:00 and I'm out of money." M walks over and gets the same spiel. We all go back to get milk and we are upset since that was our money to get dinner. There were 2 guys in line when we left,and D spent the whole time saying that if the second guy got his check cashed he was going to go off. We get back, M and S go to check out while me and D go by the area they use to cash checks(now called CC). Second guy gets his check cashed, and D says rather loudly to me "Guess she found some more money". I agree. We leave some more passive aggressive comments then leave. I can't tell if we are in the wrong or not, are we wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

Here is why:

1. You arrived at the absolute last second
Arriving at 7:59 PM for a service that closes at 8:00 PM-especially when there is already a line-is cutting it too close. Check cashing takes several minutes per person (verifying ID, entering information, printing, counting cash). The worker had to draw the line somewhere so she could balance her drawer and go home on time. The people already in line before you got served; you were behind the cutoff.

2. "Out of money" is relative to the check amount
Registers have strict cash limits at the end of a shift, and check-cashing desks frequently do cash drops to keep limited amounts on hand for safety. If your dad's check was for $500 and the next guy's check was for $60, she genuinely may not have had enough cash in the drawer for your dad's check, but had just enough for the other person.

3. Your reaction was immature and hostile
 The labeling: Calling an hourly retail worker a "B****" in your post simply for doing her job and enforcing closing times shows a lack of respect.
 The hovering and comments: Hovering around the counter to monitor her transactions and loudly making passive-aggressive remarks ("Guess she found some more money") is childish and intimidating behavior aimed at someone who cannot easily argue back without risking their job.

It is completely understandable to feel stressed and frustrated when you need that money for dinner, but taking that frustration out on a retail employee who is just following closing protocol makes you in the wrong here.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong.

I can completely understand why your family felt upset in that moment. As you mentioned, you were counting on that money to buy dinner, and I agree that seeing the next person get their check cashed after you were told the desk was closed and out of funds would feel very frustrating.

However, looking at the situation from the store's perspective, I think the employee was just doing her job:

 Timing: Arriving at 7:59 PM for a service that closes at 8:00 PM-especially when there are already people waiting-seems to be cutting it too close. Processing a check takes several minutes to verify ID and count cash, and workers sometimes have to set a firm cutoff so they can balance their registers and finish their shifts on time.
 Cash availability: "Out of money" is often relative to the specific amount written on a check. For safety reasons, registers have strict cash limits, so it seems possible she simply didn't have enough funds left in her drawer to cover your dad's amount, but had enough for a smaller check.
* The response: While it is natural to feel annoyed, it is much better to treat retail staff with patience. Hovering near the counter to monitor her, making loud passive-aggressive remarks, and calling the worker names takes out understandable personal stress on an employee who was likely just adhering to store closing policies.

title: Am I wrong for not apologising when my daughter grabbed another kids toy? My daughter who is 8 was walking with me in an
post:
Am I wrong for not apologising when my daughter grabbed another kids toy? My daughter who is 8 was walking with me in an amusement park and she saw another kid about the same size with a flashing necklace thing around her neck. My daughter ran up to the kid and grabbed it just to look at it. She was like 'wow cool'. The kid yelled and moved back and made such a huge scene where there didn't need to be. My daughter quickly dropped it and looked upset.

The mom huffed and gave me the side eye but didn't dare say anything to me.

I told my mom about it today and she called me in the wrong and that I need to check my attitude.
base:
You're in the wrong. Your mom is completely right, and you need a major attitude check.

Here is why:

1. Your daughter invaded a stranger's personal space: The necklace was around the other child's neck. Grabbing something off another person's body without asking is not okay-it is invasive, startling, and could have choked or hurt the other kid.
2. Your daughter is 8, not a toddler: An 8-year-old is old enough to understand personal boundaries and knows you must ask before touching other people or their belongings.
3. The other child's reaction was completely justified: A stranger ran up, invaded her personal space, and put their hands near her throat/chest. Yelling and backing away is a completely natural reaction to feeling startled or threatened. She didn't "make a scene"; she reacted to being grabbed.
4. You failed to parent in that moment: When your child does something inappropriate, your job as a parent is to step in, use it as a teachable moment for your child, and offer a basic, polite apology to the other family (e.g., "I'm so sorry, she was just excited to see your necklace, but she knows she shouldn't touch people without asking. Are you okay?").
5. Your hostile attitude: Saying the other mother "didn't dare say anything to me" sounds aggressively defensive. You were the one in the wrong. The other mother was likely just shocked by your daughter's behavior and your lack of basic manners.

Teach your daughter about personal boundaries and consent, and lead by example by learning how to apologize when you or your child make a mistake.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong.

I can understand that your daughter was likely just excited and curious to look at the flashing necklace, and I hear that it felt to you like the other child made an unnecessary scene. However, I think your mother makes a valid point here.

Here is why it seems like an apology was needed:

1. Personal space and safety: Because the necklace was physically around the other child's neck, running up and grabbing it can easily feel startling, invasive, and potentially unsafe.
2. Age-appropriate boundaries: At 8 years old, it seems fair to expect that a child can understand the importance of asking before touching someone else or their belongings.
3. The other child's reaction: When a stranger suddenly reaches toward someone's neck or chest, yelling and stepping back is a very natural and understandable reaction to feeling surprised or threatened.
4. The opportunity to guide your child: In moments like these, it is really helpful to step in, offer a quick and courteous apology to the other family, and use the situation as a constructive learning moment for your daughter about respecting personal space.
5. Managing defensiveness: It seems like thinking the other mother "didn't dare" say anything comes across as unnecessarily defensive. It is more likely that she was simply startled by what happened and hoped for a standard polite acknowledgment.

Taking responsibility and offering a simple apology when a mistake happens is a great way to model good manners and healthy boundaries for your daughter.

Am I wrong for treating my favourite at work differently to other staff Am I wrong for rewarding staff I deem to work harder than the people I think are slacking off.

So I work in a busy restaurant, I'm related to the owner and head chef but only work one day a week, the busiest day.

So there are numerous staff that work under me on this day and there are some I think don't work as hard as others, one girl in particular I really like and think she's just damn good.

So at the end of the shift this girl often asks for a dessert or some dinner etc, I am more than happy to oblige as I feel she deserves it. Now there are 2 other staff members who I think are slackers so I make a point of putting all the food away before they get chance to ask, I see it as rewarding the hard workers.

Recently another chef who is on my level quizzed me about why I never make anything for these 2. I say I reward the hard worker, she says the other 2 are equally hard working but we just don't see it because they work out front and tend to avoid the kitchen for some reason.

So am I the hole for looking after my favourite?
base:
You're in the wrong.

Here is why:

1. You only work one day a week and can't see the full picture
You work a single shift per week, whereas other staff and managers see the daily grind. Judging someone's overall work ethic when you are only there 14% of the week is unfair. As your peer chef pointed out, Front of House (FOH) staff do their hardest work on the floor, dealing with customers out of your sight.

2. Being related to the owner magnifies the problem
Because you are related to the owner/head chef, your behavior carries extra weight. Playing obvious favorites and treating certain employees poorly creates a toxic, morale-killing environment. It looks like nepotistic bullying to the staff who are on the receiving end.

3. Deliberately rushing to put food away is petty
There is a difference between rewarding a good employee and going out of your way to actively exclude and freeze out others. Rushing to pack everything away specifically so two people can't ask is passive-aggressive and unprofessional for someone in a supervisory role.

4. You are causing the very behavior you dislike
Your peer mentioned that the other two workers "tend to avoid the kitchen for some reason." The reason is likely you. If they know you play favorites and treat them with hostility, of course they are going to stay out of the kitchen.

---

What to do instead:
 Create an equal policy: Either shift meals/treats are an open perk for everyone working the close, or they aren't.
 Address performance properly: If people are genuinely slacking off, that requires communication, coaching, or formal feedback-not passive-aggressive food withholding.
* Listen to your peers: The chef who works alongside you regularly just told you that your perception is wrong. Believe them.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong

I think your underlying goal makes sense: it is natural to want to acknowledge and reward staff when you see them working hard during a busy shift. However, in this situation, the way it is being handled is creating unfairness.

Here is why:

 Limited visibility: Working one day a week makes it difficult to see the full scope of everyone's contributions. As your peer chef pointed out, front-of-house staff do the vast majority of their demanding work out on the floor away from the kitchen. It seems very possible they are working just as hard out of your direct line of sight.
 Impact of family ties: Because of your relationship to the owner and head chef, your actions carry extra weight. Showing obvious preference to one person while freezing out others can quickly harm overall team morale and give the appearance of favoritism.
 Directness over exclusion: Rushing to pack food away specifically so certain staff cannot ask for dinner is passive-aggressive. In a leadership role, team members benefit much more from clear, direct communication about performance rather than subtle exclusion.
 Workplace atmosphere: The fact that these staff members tend to avoid the kitchen may simply be a response to sensing that they are treated differently when they enter that space.

A more constructive approach:
 Set consistent standards: It works best when end-of-shift perks, like meals or desserts, are applied equally and transparently to everyone finishing the shift.
 Address performance openly: If there are genuine concerns about anyone slacking off, the most helpful path is direct coaching and feedback rather than withholding food.
* Value peer feedback: Taking in the perspective of the chef who works alongside you regularly can give you a more complete picture of how the entire team operates.

base:

2. You crossed the line into being a bully and a scammer: Instead of standing your ground, walking away, or ignoring him, you actively lied to him and used his mobile data/hotspot under false pretenses.

You took advantage of a kid who is clearly desperate for friends, extracted something of value from him (his internet data and battery), and gave him false hope just to use him.

When he realizes you lied to him, it's going to make him feel ten times worse than a simple "no" ever would have. You didn't just set a boundary-you exploited someone who was already down.

If you want him to leave you alone, you need to be firm: "We are not letting you in, please stop asking." But what you did was cruel and manipulative.
