title: Am I wrong for clarifying that an iced coffee is cold? The family and I stopped at Dunkin Donuts for some morning bevera
post:
Am I wrong for clarifying that an iced coffee is cold? The family and I stopped at Dunkin Donuts for some morning beverages. When placing her order my wife asked for an iced latte. The person taking our order then asked if she wanted that hot or cold. I interrupted the exchange to say "an iced latte is cold." I immediately got the death stare from my wife and I'm sure the employee saw it and I didn't say anything else.

Afterward my wife yelled at me for being so rude. I defended my case by saying her job was to take your order. When someone orders an iced drink it isn't necessary to immediately ask if they want it hot or cold. So she must not have been paying attention. I also reminded her that I am a smart by nature and I didn't really mean anything by it. But you could see a downshift in the employees upbeat attitude afterward.

I think I could've diffused the situation at the time but my wife reacted so quickly that I didn't have a chance to follow up with the "I'm just messing with ya." And I think she certainly did deserve to be messed with but I wasn't trying to ruin her morning.

So am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

Here is why:

1. Autopilot happens: Fast food and service workers repeat the same prompts hundreds of times a day ("Hot or iced?", "For here or to go?"). It was a harmless slip of the tongue or a momentary brain lapse. A simple, polite, "Cold/iced, please!" would have taken one second and kept the interaction pleasant.

2. You were punching down: Service workers are in a position where they have to remain polite and cannot easily banter back or defend themselves. Saying that she "certainly did deserve to be messed with" because she made a tiny verbal mistake is condescending and unkind.

3. "I'm just a smart-a**" isn't an excuse: Using "I'm just a smart-a** by nature" is a classic way to excuse rude behavior. Adding "I'm just messing with ya" rarely makes a customer's sarcastic remark feel like a fun joke to a worker-it usually just feels like an awkward cover-up for being snarky.

4. You ruined the vibe: You noticed yourself that the employee's upbeat attitude immediately dropped, and your wife was embarrassed by your behavior.

Next time, extend a little grace to people working customer service jobs. A simple autopilot slip-up doesn't require a public correction.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong

I can certainly agree that an iced latte is, by definition, cold, so hearing that follow-up question probably felt completely redundant. I also hear that you weren't trying to ruin anyone's morning and were just leaning into your natural tendency to be a smart-a**.

However, I still think your reaction crossed the line into unhelpful territory, for a few reasons:

1. Autopilot happens: People in customer service repeat hundreds of similar routine prompts every shift. It seems likely this was just a harmless slip of the tongue. A simple, polite "Cold, please!" would have easily kept the interaction moving forward in a pleasant way.

2. The dynamic matters: Because service workers are expected to stay professional and can't easily banter back, it's best to be gentle with them. Even if you felt she made an obvious mistake, thinking she "deserved to be messed with" can feel less like lighthearted fun and more like being condescended to.

3. Intent versus impact: While you may have intended it as a joke, saying "I'm just a smart-a**" or following up with "I'm just messing with ya" rarely lands well across a service counter. It often just comes across as an awkward cover for a snarky comment.

4. The atmosphere shifted: As you observed, the upbeat mood dropped right after your comment, and your wife felt uncomfortable with how it went down.

In the future, offering a bit of extra grace during minor slip-ups helps keep the morning positive and pleasant for everyone involved.

title: Am I wrong for refusing to replace a drink that my toddler knocked over because the girl was rude I was at baggage claim
post:
Am I wrong for refusing to replace a drink that my toddler knocked over because the girl was rude I was at baggage claim at the airport with my son, who's 3. We were leaving and as we're walking away, this girl yells "excuse me!" At me. I turn and she points to her Starbucks drink which is spilled on the floor and says "your kid did that."

I ask my son if he spilled it and he said he bumped it. The girl says "it was $5" and looks at me expectantly. I was angry about how rude she was and the way she was just looking at me and expecting me to pay for her mocha frappa-whatever without even asking, so I just shrugged and walked away. My partner called me in the wrong when I told her the story. Am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

Here is why:

1. You are responsible for the damage your child causes
When you have a toddler, part of parenting is taking responsibility for their accidents. Your son admitted he bumped into it and spilled it. The universal rule of public spaces is simple: if your kid breaks or ruins someone else's property, you replace it or apologize and offer to make it right.

2. Her reaction was understandable
Airport travel is stressful, and getting a coffee at an airport usually involves waiting in a long line and paying airport prices. Her drink was ruined, and the person responsible was walking away.

Saying "Excuse me, your kid did that. It was $5" isn't overly polite, but it's completely factual. She didn't curse at you or insult your child. Expecting a victim of an accident to use a cheerful, polite tone just to get you to take basic accountability is unreasonable.

3. You set a poor example
Dismissing her item as a "mocha frappa-whatever" and shrugging before walking away was petty. It showed your child that if you cause an accident, you can just ignore the consequences if you don't like the other person's attitude.

Your partner was right. The mature response would have been: "I am so sorry about that, he's still clumsy. Here is $5 to replace it."
rewrite:
You're in the wrong.

I can understand why her approach felt frustrating. You noted that she yelled to get your attention and bluntly told you the cost while looking at you expectantly, rather than asking nicely. You're right that her delivery wasn't particularly polite.

However, I think you were still responsible for replacing the drink. Here is why:

1. Taking responsibility for accidents: Toddlers naturally bump into things, and when an accident happens, it falls on the parent to help fix it. Since your son confirmed that he bumped the drink, offering an apology and replacing the item is the standard way to resolve the damage.
2. Considering the stressful environment: Traveling through an airport is often exhausting, and having a beverage spilled right at baggage claim can easily cause frustration. While her response was very blunt, she kept it factual and did not insult you or your child. It seems unfair to require someone to be perfectly cheerful after losing their item before agreeing to make things right.
3. Modeling positive behavior: Choosing to repair the situation even when the other person is curt is a constructive way to show your son how to handle mistakes and take accountability in public spaces.

The ideal way to handle this would have been to simply say, "I'm so sorry about that, he's still small and clumsy. Here is $5 to replace your drink." Shrugging and walking away left her with the loss from an accident your child caused, which is why your partner's assessment was correct.

title: Am I wrong for not wanting to try salvaging my project with my colleague? Basically, my colleague and I are doing a proj
post:
Am I wrong for not wanting to try salvaging my project with my colleague? Basically, my colleague and I are doing a project for one of our curricular units in Uni; unfortunately, we discovered yesterday night that, according to two friends, we have a lot to do than what we thought - we had maybe 20% of what we needed to get a 50% grade. With the amount of work left to do within 2 days before the deadline, I lost motivation to keep trying. I even inicially suggested to my colleague that we should seek help, but she decided against it, saying we didn't have anything that could be helped on.

After giving it some thought, and discovering that flunking the curricular unit has no repercussions other than having to repeat it next year, I wanted to save myself the hassle and just flunk the unit and try to get a better grade next time, rather than delivering something half-assed. Both my colleague and I really like to have high grades, but she wants to keep trying... We would just barely get a positive grade though (a 50% out of 100%, in this case).

At least, from my perspective, the positives outweigh the negatives when it comes to trying again next year (I would even have less curricular units next year to worry about, having 3 instead of the usual 5, so more time to prepare for it and study), but my colleague and my parents are not happy whatsoever with my decision. am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

Here is why:

1. You are making a unilateral decision that tanks someone else.
If this were an individual assignment, you would be completely free to make the strategic choice to fail, drop the unit, and retake it next year for a better grade.

However, this is a group project. Your decision doesn't just affect you; it directly sabotages your partner. You decided that failing is "no big deal" because you have a lighter course load next year. Your partner clearly does not want to waste an entire semester of work, spend money/time retaking a class, or delay their graduation. By giving up, you are forcing your decision onto them.

2. You owe it to your partner to put in the work until the deadline.
There are still two days left. In university time, 48 hours of focused work can be the difference between a 30% and a 55%. Even if the end result is a barely passing grade, your partner has every right to want that pass and move on with their life.

Quitting 48 hours before a deadline leaves your partner in an impossible situation: either do the work of two people in two days, or fail because their teammate gave up.

What you should do:
 Hunker down and help: Put your personal preferences aside for the next two days, grind through the work with your colleague, and submit the best possible version you can manage.
 Look into retake policies: In many universities, if you pass with a low grade (like 50%), you can still apply for a grade improvement/retake exam later if you truly care about your GPA, without dragging your partner down with you.

You made a commitment to a team. You don't get to quit just because failing is convenient for you.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong.

I acknowledge your perspective that taking a failing grade now and retaking the unit next year feels like a better strategic choice for you, especially given your goal of achieving higher marks and having a lighter course load next term. I think we can agree that if this were an individual project, deciding to retake a class for a better grade would be a completely reasonable decision.

However, it seems important to remember that this is a shared project where your actions directly shape your partner's outcome. While flunking might fit your plans, your colleague wants to keep trying to secure a passing grade so she does not have to spend additional time or resources repeating the course. Making a unilateral decision to stop working effectively leaves her in a position where she either has to do the work of two people in two days or fail against her wishes.

With two days remaining, focused effort can still be enough to reach that passing mark. It is much better to honor your commitment to your teammate by working together through the deadline to submit the best project you can manage. Once the assignment is turned in, you can always check your university's policies to see if individual grade improvement exams are an option for you later without hindering your partner's progress.

title: Am I wrong for refusing to go to prom with my gf My (19M) girlfriend (17F) and I have been dating for a year and a half.
post: Am I wrong for refusing to go to prom with my gf My (19M) girlfriend (17F) and I have been dating for a year and a half. She is currently a senior in high school. Last year when she was a junior, I told her I'd go to prom with her but a family vacation came up and I couldn't go with her. This year, I told her I wouldn't go with her again because I will be 2 years older than everyone there which makes me uncomfortable, and I've always hated school dances. She is upset because all her friends will have dates so she doesn't want to go and be the only one without a date, but it's really important for her to go to her senior prom.
base:
You're in the wrong, gently.

Here is why:

1. The age excuse doesn't really hold up
You are 19, and she is a 17-year-old senior. Most high school seniors are 17-18, and some are already 19. A 19-year-old attending senior prom with their high school girlfriend is completely normal, happens all the time, and no one will bat an eye or think it's weird.

2. You already bailed on her once
You promised to go with her for her junior prom and couldn't make it. While a family vacation might have been out of your control, the result was that she missed out on experiencing prom with her boyfriend last year. Bailing on her senior prom-which is her absolute last chance to experience this milestone-makes it feel like you simply don't care about things that matter to her.

3. Relationships require small sacrifices
Part of being in a mature relationship is showing up for your partner on days that are important to them, even if the event isn't your personal cup of tea. Prom is one single evening-about 4 to 5 hours of your life.

You don't have to love school dances to put on a nice suit, take pictures with her, make her feel beautiful, eat dinner, and stand by her side so she isn't the only one in her friend group without her partner there.

The Bottom Line
To you, it's just an annoying high school dance you've outgrown. To her, it's a once-in-a-lifetime high school milestone with her friends that she wants to share with the person she loves. Sucking it up for a few hours to make your girlfriend happy is basic relationship courtesy.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong, gently.

I hear that you feel uncomfortable attending because you are 19 and have always disliked school dances, and it makes complete sense that going to a high school event after you've already graduated might feel awkward.

However, I think it might help to keep a few perspectives in mind:

 The age difference is very standard: High school seniors are generally 17 to 18, and some are 19. It seems very common for a 19-year-old partner to attend a senior prom, and it is unlikely anyone there would view it as out of place.
 This is her final high school milestone: As you mentioned, you weren't able to attend her junior prom due to a family trip. Because of that, senior prom is her last chance to experience this event, and she really wants to share it with you rather than be the only person in her group without her partner.
* It is an opportunity to support your partner: Relationships often thrive when we make small compromises for the people we care about. Even if dances aren't your favorite environment, spending four or five hours to dress up, take photos, share dinner, and stand by her side can mean the world to her.

While prom might feel like just an event you've outgrown, it seems to be a meaningful milestone for your girlfriend. Being there for one evening is a wonderful way to show your care and support for her.

title: Am I wrong for giving an overly exuberant and potentially very rude response? Flew to LA with some friends from the east
post:
Am I wrong for giving an overly exuberant and potentially very rude response? Flew to LA with some friends from the east coast to see Hamilton (the play). I was SO excited. Amped up. My buddy and I had seen it on Broadway in New York in April and have been listening to it non stop since then.

This excitement leads to me to use some very enthusiastic body gestures in the lobby while everyone is coming in and I end up elbowing someone pretty decently. More than a brush but less than a shove. I spun around to apologize as soon as it happened but before I could spit it out the woman I elbowed looked at me and said "Jesus!". She was angry.

I couldn't help myself. My filter was already gone. Excitement was high. I found her preemptive response mildly annoying - I exclaim, in a bit of a sarcastic tone, "Jesus Christ!". She looks like she is about to kill me. It is too late. Even my aloof friends notice her death glare. I do the equivalent of whistling looking around and pretending nothing happened until she walks away.

Was I in the wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

Here is the breakdown of why:

1. Lack of spatial awareness: Being excited about a show is great, but a crowded theater lobby is not the place for wild, flailing gestures. You hit a stranger "pretty decently." That's entirely on you.
2. Her reaction was normal: Saying "Jesus!" when an unexpected elbow strikes you out of nowhere is a completely reasonable, involuntary reaction to sudden physical impact. It wasn't a "preemptive response"; it was a direct reaction to being hit.
3. Your retort was rude: Mocking someone you just struck-instead of immediately saying, "I am so sorry, that was totally my fault, I was talking with my hands"-instantly turned an innocent accident into an aggressive interaction.
4. The non-apology: Pretending it didn't happen and whistling while she glared at you just put the cherry on the cake.

You let your adrenaline and lack of a filter override basic public manners. You owe that woman an imaginary apology into the universe.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong

I definitely agree that being amped up to see a show you love is completely natural. I also hear that you originally intended to apologize, but felt annoyed when she exclaimed "Jesus!" before you could get the words out.

However, I think you are in the wrong here for a few key reasons:

1. Spatial awareness: It seems easy to lose track of our surroundings when we're excited, but crowded theater lobbies require being mindful of shared space. The accidental hit was entirely on you.
2. Her reaction: When someone gets struck out of nowhere, an exclamation like "Jesus!" is a very standard, involuntary reaction to physical impact rather than a preemptive slight.
3. The retort: Responding with sarcasm instead of following through with a sincere apology turns an innocent accident into an intentionally rude moment. Offering a quick, straightforward "I'm so sorry, that was totally my fault" is the most constructive way to clear the air.
4. The brush-off: Pretending nothing happened and looking away leaves the situation tense and unresolved, rather than setting things right.

High energy can sometimes get the better of our filters, but in tight public spaces, staying accountable and offering a genuine apology goes a long way.

title: Am I wrong for not throwing away my coffee pods? So someone at the office left a Post-It note on the Keurig asking peopl
post: Am I wrong for not throwing away my coffee pods? So someone at the office left a Post-It note on the Keurig asking people to throw away their used coffee pods after making coffee. I (and most people at the office, for that matter) usually just leave them in when done and just throw away the one that was in there already before making some.
base:
You're in the wrong.

While this is a very common office habit, it is actually poor shared-kitchen etiquette for several reasons:

1. The Hot Water / Tea Drinkers
The biggest victims of the "leave it in" method are people who use the Keurig to dispense hot water for tea, oatmeal, soup, or instant noodles.
 If they don't check inside first, they end up with coffee-flavored hot water.
 Even if they do check, they are forced to handle your hot, soggy, dripping trash just to get a cup of plain water.

2. Hygiene and Mold
A used coffee pod is warm, dark, and soaking wet. Leaving it trapped inside the sealed Keurig chamber creates an ideal breeding ground for mold and bacteria, especially if the machine sits unused overnight or over a weekend.

3. Machine Maintenance
Leaving the pod inside keeps the exit needles embedded in wet grounds for extended periods. As the grounds cool and dry, they can stick to the needles, leading to clogs, coffee grounds in subsequent cups, and a shorter lifespan for the machine.

4. Basic Office Etiquette
The universal rule of shared spaces is to clean up after yourself immediately, not leave your mess for the next person to deal with. Lifting the handle, letting the pod drop into the bin (or grabbing it and tossing it in the trash), takes literally two seconds.

The Verdict: Even if "everyone was doing it," now that someone has pointed it out, the polite and sanitary move is to simply toss your pod when you're done brewing.
rewrite:
You're slightly in the wrong.

I agree that this is a very common office habit, and I understand that leaving the pod in place and just swapping it before your next cup feels like an easy, practical routine when most of your coworkers do the same.

However, I think switching to tossing the pod immediately after brewing is the better practice for a shared kitchen, for a few key reasons:

 Supporting tea and hot water users: People sometimes use the Keurig just for hot water for tea, oatmeal, or soup. Leaving the chamber empty ensures they get clean water without coffee flavor, and without having to handle a used, dripping pod.
 Hygiene: A warm, wet pod left inside a closed chamber can sometimes create an environment for mold or bacteria to grow, especially if the machine sits idle overnight or over a weekend.
 Machine care: Removing the pod right away keeps the needles clear and helps prevent wet grounds from drying, sticking, and causing clogs over time.
 Shared space etiquette: Taking a couple of seconds to discard the pod as soon as your cup is ready leaves the machine fresh and ready to go for whoever walks up next.

Now that a coworker has raised the issue, making the quick effort to throw the pod away when you finish brewing seems like a small, positive step to keep the kitchen clean and considerate for everyone.

title: Am I wrong for telling my friend that he needs to get over his ex-girlfriend by playing the field? My coworker, 26, rece
post:
Am I wrong for telling my friend that he needs to get over his ex-girlfriend by playing the field? My coworker, 26, recently broke up with his girlfriend of 5 years. He was super in love with her, but they broke up because she travelled too much for work. He was also planning to propose to her but she wanted to experience more of life before settling down.

He was telling me all this at the pub over a beer. He looked absolutely miserable, and said it's been a month but he misses her so much still. He said he was sure that she was "the one".

I told him there's no such thing as "the one". I said, you know what, you're a handsome, male model-esque guy and any girl would be lucky to have you. I told him to "play the field", party, sleep around, celebrate his newfound freedom, etc. I said he's still young and he doesn't need to think about marriage until his 30s.

He said he "wasn't sure" that playing the field is what is best for him. I told him that's nonsense, unless he prefers moping around as an alternative. He said he can't even imagine being with any other woman, that nobody else will measure up to her beauty or her personality. I said, yeah sure's she's pretty but there's hundreds of other pretty girls in this city. I said he's being ridiculous by focusing so much on her and should take my advice.

He said my advice is really douchey and he says he can't believe I would suggest something like that as a legitimate way of healing.

Am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

While your initial intention might have been to hype him up and make him feel desirable, your delivery and complete lack of empathy make you in the wrong here.

Here is why your friend is upset with you:

1. The timeline: They were together for five years and he was planning to propose. It has only been one month. Being heartbroken after one month is not "moping around"-it is completely normal, healthy grieving. Expecting him to snap out of a half-decade relationship in four weeks is completely unrealistic.
2. You completely invalidated his feelings: Calling his emotions "nonsense" and telling him he's being "ridiculous" when he opened up to you is terrible friend behavior. He was looking for support and a listening ear, not to be belittled.
3. Your advice isn't universally good: "Sleeping around" and "partying" might be how you handle breakups, but for many people-especially relationship-oriented people who are deeply in love-casual sex while emotionally devastated just makes them feel empty, guilty, and worse.
4. You doubled down: Offering a different perspective is one thing. But when he explicitly told you that wasn't what he wanted or needed, you aggressively pushed it and insulted his process.

He called your advice "douchey" because it was douchey. You treated a major life heartbreak like a minor inconvenience that can be cured with a few one-night stands.

If you value this friendship, you should reach out and say: "Hey, I'm sorry for how I handled our conversation. I was trying to cheer you up and remind you of your worth, but I ended up dismissing your pain. Take all the time you need to heal, and I'm here if you just need to vent."
rewrite:
You're in the wrong.

I think it is understandable that you wanted to hype your friend up and remind him of his worth, and I agree that pointing out his positive qualities comes from wanting him to feel better. You see him as a young, attractive guy with a lot of options, and you wanted to help pull him out of his misery.

However, it seems your delivery ended up doing the opposite of supporting him, for a few key reasons:

1. The timeline needs space: A five-year relationship where he was planning to propose is a significant bond. After just one month, feeling heartbroken is a completely natural part of grieving that loss, rather than simply "moping around." It takes time to heal from something so serious.
2. Support over dismissal: When a friend opens up about deep pain, I think what they need most is a listening ear. Telling him his feelings are "nonsense" or that he is being "ridiculous" dismisses the very real grief he is experiencing.
3. Different paths to healing: While partying or casual dating might feel helpful to some people, for someone who is deeply relationship-oriented and heartbroken, it can sometimes feel empty and make them feel worse.
4. Respecting his perspective: When he explained that playing the field wasn't what was best for him, it would have been more supportive to accept his boundary instead of pushing the advice and insisting he follow it.

If you value the friendship, it might be best to reach out with something like: "Hey, I'm sorry for how I handled our conversation. I was trying to cheer you up and remind you of your worth, but I realize I ended up dismissing your pain. Take all the time you need to heal, and I'm here if you just want to talk."

Am I wrong for not letting my gf study with me? It's exam time. I have an exam tomorrow, my girlfriends are next week. I prefer to study alone. My gf doesn't understand why we can't study together sometimes, but it's just the way I like it.
I've been studying hard for these exams so I haven't seen my girlfriend much (once last week, once this week so far)
There have been power cuts at my girlfriends house starting from yesterday, meaning she can't study (no WiFi, no light) so today she asked could she study here. I want to study alone so I said no, sorry. Now she's upset, Am I wrong?
base:
You're in the wrong.

Here is why:

Under normal circumstances, you have every right to set boundaries around how you study. If she was just asking to hang out and do a "study date," you would be completely justified in saying no so you can focus on your exam tomorrow.

However, this wasn't a normal circumstance-it was an emergency.

She literally has no power, light, or Wi-Fi during exam season, making it impossible for her to prepare for her own tests. Instead of treating her request as a partner in need of a functional workspace, you treated it as an inconvenience to your preference.

Why you're in the wrong:
1. You prioritized a preference over her necessity: You prefer to be alone; she needed electricity and internet to pass her exams.
2. You offered zero compromise: You could have easily said, "You can come over to use the Wi-Fi and power, but I have to be completely locked in. You can work in the living room/kitchen and I will stay in my bedroom with the door shut. We can't talk or hang out until after my exam."
3. Lack of partnership: Being in a relationship means showing up for each other when things go wrong. Leaving your girlfriend in the dark (literally) during finals week when you had the resources to help her shows a serious lack of empathy and support.

How to fix it:
Reach out, apologize, and explain that you were panicked and stressed about your exam tomorrow, but recognize that you were selfish. Offer to let her use your space/Wi-Fi in a separate room under strict, quiet study rules so you both can succeed.

title: Am I wrong for laughing at my missing childhood acquaintance? So bit of background information:
post:
Am I wrong for laughing at my missing childhood acquaintance? So bit of background information:
I'm in a group chat with everyone of my lower school class' members. Really fun, and really nice to still be in contact with them. However, there's 1 guy who isn't in the group chat. I heard he's a junkie now, and somewhat on the criminal path. Nobody has heard of him for years.

So, an hour ago, my local police put out a message on their twitter that this particular guy was missing, and there's a search team actively looking for him (including a photo of his face). Someone in the group chat made a screenshot of the tweet. The tweet stated that this guy was missing and said he was last seen wearing a black coat, brown pants and white crocs.

When reading this, I kinda had to laugh because of the white crocs. This was also my response to the screenshot sent into the group chat:

'Wow, What?!'
'Kinda had to laugh because of the white crocs tho'
'But damn'

Now everyone in the group chat is saying I'm insensitive and there's a guy missing, and god knows what happened to him

So, Am I wrong for laughing at my missing childhood acquaintance?
base:
You're in the wrong, but mostly for being tone-deaf rather than malicious.

Here is the breakdown of why your group chat reacted the way they did:

1. Inside thoughts vs. Outside thoughts: It is a normal human reaction to find absurd details funny-a serious police alert mentioning "white Crocs" creates cognitive dissonance, and the mental image can make you chuckle internally. However, you shouldn't have typed it out.
2. Context and timing matter: This isn't a funny meme or a random stranger on the news; it is a childhood classmate who is struggling with addiction and is actively missing with a search team looking for him. Given his background, there is a very real possibility he is in grave danger, injured, or dead.
3. "Reading the room": Your group chat was likely processing shock, sadness, or concern for someone they used to know. Dropping a "lol white crocs" comment in the middle of that makes you seem callous, indifferent, and lacking empathy.

You didn't laugh because he was missing, but by vocalizing your amusement about his shoes, you minimized a potentially tragic situation.

What to do now:
A simple, genuine apology to the group will clear the air. Something like:
""You're right, that was insensitive of me. My brain just latched onto a weird detail in the description, but I realize the timing was awful and this is a serious situation. I really hope he's found safe.""
rewrite:
You're in the wrong, though it seems this was more tone-deaf than malicious.

I can understand how the specific detail about the white crocs caught you off guard, and as you mentioned, your reaction was about his footwear rather than the fact that someone is missing. It is sometimes a very natural human response to find an unexpected detail like that absurd or jarring.

At the same time, I think typing that reaction out in the group chat was where the misstep happened. Because an active search is currently underway and a former classmate may be in serious danger, the moment really called for care. It seems your peers were processing shock and concern for someone they used to know, so introducing humor right then can easily come across as minimizing a potentially tragic situation.

Focusing on empathy and the hope that he is found safe is the best path forward. A brief, sincere apology to the group can help clear the air:

""You're right, that was insensitive of me. My brain just latched onto an odd detail in the description, but I realize the timing was inappropriate for such a serious situation. I really hope he's found safe.""

Am I wrong for dumping my son's ice cream out On our way back from a Dr I stopped to get us ice cream at a DQ for him (2 yo) doing a good job and behaving. I ordered a blizzard for me and a "mini or less amount of vanilla" in a large cup for my son. I drove up, paid, got the blizzard flip, then out came the large cup. Filled. To. The. Top. Probably 3-4 inches over the top actually. The window person said "I gave him extra!" and handed it over.

All I could think of was him getting that all over... everything... in the car. I flipped it over and dropped it out on the pavement below and drove off.

Not to make the poor kid sad, I did pull over and share some of mine, but there was no way I was going to give him a heaping tub of ice cream unattended in the back seat.
base:
You're in the wrong - not for refusing to give a 2-year-old a mountain of ice cream in the backseat of your car (that part is just basic survival instincts), but for how you handled it.

Here is why:

1. The worker thought they were being nice: Minimum wage drive-thru workers often think they are doing a customer a solid by hooking them up with extra food. The worker had good intentions, even though they completely missed the point of why you asked for a tiny amount in a large cup.
2. You created a mess for someone else to clean: Dumping a massive mound of sticky, sugary dairy directly onto their drive-thru pavement is rude. It attracts bees, wasps, and ants right where employees have to lean out the window, and someone making $12/hour likely had to go out with a bucket of hot water or a hose to clean up after you.
3. You had so many other options:
 You could have said, "Oh, thank you so much, but he's only two! Could you actually scoop most of that out, or give me a tiny cup? Otherwise, my backseat is doomed."
 You could have just set it in your front cup holder, eaten what you wanted later, and tossed the rest in a trash can.
 * You could have held onto it and fed him a few spoonfuls yourself when you stopped.

Your logic regarding your kid was completely sound (nobody wants a soft-serve disaster in the upholstery), but aggressively dumping it on the ground in front of the worker and driving off was an over-the-top, unhinged reaction to an act of misguided generosity.
rewrite:
You're in the wrong.

I definitely agree with you that handing a mountain of ice cream to an unattended two-year-old in the back seat would lead to a huge mess. I understand that your immediate thought was preventing ice cream from getting all over your car, and keeping your upholstery clean makes complete sense.

However, I think the verdict is you're in the wrong because of how the situation was handled:

1. The employee's intent: It seems the worker genuinely thought they were doing a nice thing by offering extra, even though it completely missed the reason why you asked for a smaller amount.
2. Leaving a mess for staff: Dropping the melting ice cream directly onto the drive-thru pavement creates a sticky problem right outside the window that the employees likely had to spend time cleaning up.
3. Other ways to handle it: In these moments, it works much better to choose a different approach:
 You could simply explain the situation to the worker ("Thank you so much, but he's only two! Could you scoop most of that out or put it in a tiny cup so it doesn't end up all over the car?").
 You could place the cup in your front cup holder, keep it out of reach, and throw the excess into a trash can later.
 * You could hold onto the cup and feed him a few spoonfuls yourself when you stopped.

While your goal of avoiding a car cleanup was entirely understandable, dumping the ice cream onto the pavement at the window wasn't the right way to manage it.

title: Am I wrong for begging my bf to take a group photo with us? Okay... more like... are we tas... plural.

are buttfaces for begging? We already apologized, but he is still angry at us.
base:
You're in the wrong (you and your groupmates, though gently).

While your intentions came from a place of celebration, pride, and wanting to include him, "no" is a complete sentence.

Here is why you crossed into being in the wrong:

1. You already knew his boundary: You stated that he hates photos so much he didn't even take part in the class photo. His dislike for being photographed wasn't a secret or a surprise.
2. Group pressure feels awful: It wasn't just you asking him privately; the entire group "begged" him. Being publicly pressured and put on the spot by multiple people-especially in front of peers and a professor-feels less like an invitation and more like an ambush.
3. Intent vs. Impact: You wanted a nice memory; the impact was that you made him feel alienated and forced to defend a boundary he had already made clear.

It's completely understandable why you wanted him in the picture (you're his partner, you're proud of the win, and you love him!), but badgering someone after they decline is where it becomes disrespectful.

He is likely still angry because it feels like his friends and his girlfriend care more about a photo aesthetic/social expectation than his comfort and boundaries.

Give him a little time to cool off, and when you talk to him, don't focus on "it was just a picture." Acknowledge that you put him on the spot and pressured him, and assure him that next time he says "no," you'll respect it without making a scene.

1. His boundary was already clear: You noted that he dislikes photos so much that he didn't even participate in the class photo, so his preference wasn't unexpected.

title: Am I wrong for not correcting a cashier's mistake because it saved me some money? Every summer, I tend to have a massive

Am I wrong for not correcting a cashier's mistake because it saved me some money? Every summer, I tend to have a massive acne problem, and decided to invest in some pricey face wash.

It was early in the morning and I was at a CVS. I bought a couple of energy drinks along with the face wash. As I was ready to checkout, the cashier tried to make small talk about face wash and skin care. Ironically, I noticed she forgot to scan it. Rather than correcting her, I just kinda stood there anticipating her to figure it out (my bill came out like $3 and the face wash is like $10).

I didn't correct her. I payed and walked out with a free face wash. I've never stolen anything before that.

I find it sad that had the cashier made a mistake that would cost me, I'd immediately correct her, but since it came to my benefit, I ran with it. am I wrong?
base:
Technically, you're in the wrong -though it's a very common, relatable human reaction.

Here is why:

1. You knew in real time
There's a difference between getting home, looking at the receipt, and realizing, "Oh, they forgot to scan the face wash," versus watching it happen at the register, knowing your total was wrong, and making a conscious choice to remain silent. By doing that, you knowingly walked out with an item you didn't pay for.

2. The double standard you pointed out
You hit the nail on the head in your last paragraph: integrity is consistent.
If the cashier accidentally scanned the face wash twice and charged you $23 instead of $13, you would have spoken up immediately because it was unfair to you. Taking advantage of the mistake when the error works in your favor means you only care about transactional fairness when you're on the losing end.

The Nuance
Does this make you a terrible person or a criminal mastermind? No.
 CVS is a multi-billion-dollar corporation that accounts for inventory shrinkage, so you didn't bankrupt a small business.
 The cashier is very unlikely to get into trouble over a single $10 inventory discrepancy.

However, in the context of everyday ethics, taking advantage of an underpaid worker's momentary distraction during friendly small talk to get a free item is the wrong thing to do.

The fact that you feel guilty about it shows your moral compass is working. Use it as a learning experience for next time.
rewrite:
I think technically you're in the wrong, though it seems like a very common and understandable impulse in the moment.

Here is why:

 Knowing in real time: It seems there is a meaningful difference between finding an unscanned item on your receipt after leaving the store versus noticing the total is off at the register and choosing to stay quiet. In this case, walking out knowing the face wash was missed meant knowingly taking an item without paying for it.
 The double standard you noted: You mentioned finding it sad that you would have spoken up immediately if the error had cost you money, but ran with it because it saved you money. I agree with your insight there-integrity is about holding the same standard of fairness whether a mistake helps or hurts our wallet.

To be fair, this doesn't make you a terrible person. CVS is a massive corporation with inventory shrinkage accounted for, and the cashier is very unlikely to get into trouble over a single $10 item. However, in terms of everyday ethics, letting a worker's momentary distraction during friendly conversation result in a free item wasn't the right choice.

The fact that you are reflecting on this shows that your moral compass is active, and I think you can use this self-awareness as a positive guide for how you want to handle these situations in the future.

title: Would I be wrong if I stand in a line before we are ready to checkout? So my husband and I went to the store and we sepa

Would I be wrong if I stand in a line before we are ready to checkout? So my husband and I went to the store and we separated to each grab different items. He finished first and got in line but he got to the front of the line before I met him there so he just checked out. I told him that I would have just let the next person in line go ahead of me and not checked out so I could wait until he got back. He says he would have felt like in the wrong going that. So would I be wrong if I held my spot in line and let people go ahead of me until my husband returned?

Note: I got to the line right as he was handed his receipt so only one person would have had to go in front of him.
base:
You're slightly in the wrong (or rather, your husband handled it the right way).

Here is why your husband's instinct was correct:

1. It creates awkward bottlenecks and confusion
If this was a traditional checkout lane with a conveyor belt, standing at the front and waving people past you creates physical and social chaos. The cashier doesn't know whether to wait for you, the people behind you are hesitant because they don't want to cut, and it's awkward to shuffle past a cart/person in a narrow checkout aisle.

(The only exception is a store with a single snake-line feeding into multiple registers, like TJ Maxx or Barnes & Noble, where stepping aside is frictionless).

2. The standard rule of "Placeholding"
Social etiquette generally dictates that you don't get in line until you are ready to check out.
 Acceptable: You're actively loading your items onto the belt and your partner runs to grab one forgotten item (like butter) and makes it back in 30 seconds.
 Faux pas: Using one person as a human placeholder while the other person does a significant portion of the shopping, forcing the line to adjust around you.

3. Your husband's solution was the most efficient
By simply checking out his items:
 He kept the line moving.
 The cashier wasn't left in limbo.
* You only had to do a quick second transaction right after (or wait in a short line), which takes virtually the same amount of time without the social awkwardness.

Your idea was well-intentioned since you were trying to let people go ahead of you, but your husband did the polite, standard thing by just checking out his half and stepping aside.
rewrite:
You're slightly in the wrong (or rather, it seems your husband handled it the best way).

I understand your perspective that letting the next person go ahead felt like an easy fix, especially since you arrived right as he was handed his receipt and only one person would have needed to bypass him. I also agree that offering to let someone ahead of you comes from a considerate intention to avoid making others wait.

However, I think your husband's instinct was ultimately the right call for a few reasons:

 Keeping the checkout clear and comfortable: In a traditional checkout lane, standing at the front and waving someone past can sometimes cause confusion. The cashier may be unsure whether to begin scanning, and other shoppers might feel hesitant or awkward trying to squeeze past a cart in a narrow space. (The main exception would be a single snake-line feeding into multiple registers, where stepping aside tends to be seamless.)
 Standard line expectations: Etiquette generally works best when people enter the line once they are fully ready to pay. While having someone grab one quick forgotten item while items are being scanned is usually fine, holding a place while part of the shopping is still being completed can make things complicated for the line behind you.
* Simple efficiency: By completing his transaction, your husband kept the register moving and left no ambiguity for the cashier. Taking care of your remaining items in a quick second transaction is often just as fast, while keeping the flow smooth and comfortable for everyone.
